item.title: Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had a relationship with a second employee, sources say
item.description: The revelation follows two other extramarital affairs that led to his resignation on Nov 12.
item.dc:creator: The Straits Times
item.content:encoded:
Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had a relationship with a second employee, sources say Sign up now: Get ST's newsletters delivered to your inbox

The former Nvidia chief executive officer’s decision to resign from the company could disrupt the AI industry that he helped shape. PHOTO: REUTERS

Published   Nov 13, 2026, 09:05 AM

Updated   Nov 13, 2026, 09:11 AM

Set as preferred source

Listen Summarise

Jensen Huang, former Nvidia CEO, resigned after reports of affairs with two employees, including Alice Huang and Kimberly Powell, according to Reuters sources. Reuters says a second relationship was revealed, adding pressure on Huang and raising questions about possible foreign intelligence targeting. Nvidia named finance chief Colette Kress interim CEO and started a search for a permanent replacement; shares fell 5.5% on Nov 12.

AI generated

SAN FRANCISCO – Ousted Nvidia chief executive officer Jensen Huang had an intimate relationship with a second employee, according to two people familiar with the matter, Reuters has learnt. The revelation follows two other extramarital affairs that led to his resignation on Nov 12 . The two women are Alice Huang, who US intelligence suspects of being a Chinese spy , and Kimberly Powell, Nvidia’s vice-president of health care. Reuters is not naming the second employee. Attempts to reach the woman were not successful.

Nvidia declined to comment. Powell, Jensen Huang and a representative for Nvidia’s board did not reply to requests for comment. Alice Huang could not be reached for comment. Jensen Huang admitted to an affair in a Nov 8 statement following the reports of his relationship with Alice Huang, without referring to her by name. The former Nvidia chief executive officer’s decision to resign from the company could disrupt the AI industry that he helped shape. Nvidia has used its financial strength to help create an industry around AI through complex financial arrangements that ease the purchase of the company’s chips. It has backed cloud computing companies and AI labs in order to do so.

Pressure on Jensen Huang, who is 63 and married, to resign mounted after reports of his affair with Alice Huang. Nvidia’s board has appointed finance chief Colette Kress as interim chief executive officer while it conducts a search to replace Jensen Huang. The board is considering internal and external candidates for the job. Earlier in November, Nvidia’s board launched a probe, led by independent directors with outside legal counsel, into whether Jensen Huang had been targeted by a foreign intelligence operation. It also expressed confidence in him at the time.

Shares fell 5.5% on Nov 12 in active trading. The stock has shed more than 30% of its value since its early October peak. REUTERS

item.title: Jensen Huang forfeits US$108 million in unvested Nvidia equity
item.description: The relinquished awards represent roughly 0.08% of his net worth.
item.dc:creator: The Straits Times
item.content:encoded:
Jensen Huang forfeits US$108 million in unvested Nvidia equity Sign up now: Get ST's newsletters delivered to your inbox

Jensen Huang’s wealth is derived almost entirely from his holding of Nvidia’s common shares, rather than stock options or other forms of equity compensation. PHOTO: ERIC LEE/NYTIMES

Published   Nov 13, 2026, 07:00 AM

Updated   Nov 13, 2026, 07:00 AM

Set as preferred source

Summarise

Jensen Huang will lose about US$108 million in unvested Nvidia equity after leaving the company. Nvidia’s policy says unvested RSUs are forfeited when service ends. Huang’s wealth is mostly in Nvidia shares, not pay or options. Bloomberg says his net worth is US$138.4 billion, and the lost awards are only 0.08% of it. His exit followed the revelation of two extramarital affairs and hit Nvidia shares hard. The stock fell as much as 14% before closing down 4.3%, cutting more than US$6 billion from his wealth.

AI generated

Jensen Huang will forfeit about US$108 million (S$138.9 million) in unvested equity compensation after being ousted from Nvidia – a fraction of his total wealth. The relinquished awards represent roughly 0.08% of his net worth, according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index, which puts his fortune at US$138.4 billion. The company’s equity compensation policy specifies that unvested RSUs, or restricted stock units, are forfeited once an executive terminates continuous service.

He holds about 346,000 such units and would receive about 310,000 shares through the company’s equity incentive plan, assuming its performance meets certain targets. Unlike many other tech chief executive officers, Huang’s wealth is derived almost entirely from his holding of Nvidia’s common shares, rather than stock options or other forms of equity compensation. Huang controls about a 3.5% voting stake in the Santa Clara, California-based firm, which makes up nearly 97% of his wealth, according to Bloomberg’s wealth index.

Since Nvidia only has one class of shares, Huang does not hold any privileged voting rights. The 63-year-old co-founder, who stepped down following the revelation of two extramarital affairs, was paid about US$7.5 million in cash compensation in each of the past two years – a negligible sum relative to his net worth.  Still, his resignation came at an immediate cost.

Nvidia shares plunged as much as 14% in New York before paring losses to close down 4.3% at US$166.19, wiping more than US$6 billion from Huang’s net worth. BLOOMBERG

item.title: Tougher curbs on AI chip sales to China likely after Nvidia CEO resigns
item.description: There is growing consensus in Congress that favours new restrictions on chip exports to China.
item.dc:creator: The Straits Times
item.content:encoded:
Tougher curbs on AI chip sales to China likely after Nvidia CEO resigns Sign up now: Get ST's newsletters delivered to your inbox

US House Speaker Mike Johnson said on Nov 12 that the growing consensus in Congress favours new restrictions on chip exports to China. PHOTO: AFP

Published   Nov 13, 2026, 06:55 AM

Updated   Nov 13, 2026, 06:55 AM

Set as preferred source

Summarise

US lawmakers want tougher limits on advanced AI chip sales to China after scrutiny of Nvidia and former CEO Jensen Huang grew over a reported spy-linked affair. Congress is weighing new Bills to give lawmakers more control, track chips, and block allies from helping China get chip tools or maintenance. The Remote Access Security Act could hit Nvidia most, as Chinese firms already rent overseas Nvidia computing power and the company warned of a “material impact on our business.”

AI generated

WASHINGTON - US lawmakers from both parties are pushing for tougher restrictions on China’s access to advanced artificial intelligence chips following media reports about former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with a suspected Chinese spy , which has increased scrutiny of the company’s role in US national security. Huang stepped down on Nov 12, days after reports of an affair with an executive at a Singapore-based tech company whom US authorities suspect of spying for Beijing. Nvidia did not address Huang’s actions in its statement; he has admitted to an extramarital affair without naming the person. Nvidia’s advanced AI chips are widely used to develop cutting-edge AI models, making the company key to the US race against China to build superior AI systems. The US for years has sought to limit China’s access to Nvidia’s most advanced chips, though Chinese companies have repeatedly found ways around those restrictions. Huang supported allowing more exports to China.

House Speaker Mike Johnson said on Nov 12 that the growing consensus in Congress favours new restrictions on chip exports to China. Here are the proposals Congress is weighing. A handful of lawmakers want to attach them to the annual defence authorisation Bill, a must-pass measure that funds the military and typically attracts bipartisan support. A Senate version of the legislation already includes several of them, including the AI Overwatch Act, Chip Security Act and Match Act. Growing congressional authority over chip exports US law gives the Commerce Department broad authority to block or allow advanced chip exports without congressional input.

Senator Elizabeth Warren, a Democrat from Massachusetts, and Senator Jim Banks, an Indiana Republican, argue export-control decisions with major national security implications should face greater congressional oversight. Their proposed AI Overwatch Act would give Congress a larger role in reviewing changes to export rules. The measure is significant for Nvidia because it could make it harder for future administrations to loosen restrictions on sales of its advanced chips to China. Nvidia’s revenue from chip sales to Chinese data centres for now is near zero, according to an August company statement, and the company doesn’t expect that to change in the third quarter.

Tracking advanced chips The Chip Security Act seeks to address a recurring problem of advanced chips legally sold abroad but later diverted to China. The Bill would require chipmakers to track the location of advanced AI processors and notify the government if they suspect chips have reached prohibited users. For Nvidia, the measure could create new compliance costs and reporting obligations. The Semiconductor Industry Association, whose members include Nvidia, has said mandatory tracking requirements could be costly for the industry. Pressuring US allies The Match Act would pressure US allies to restrict sales and maintenance of advanced chipmaking equipment destined for China. Allies such as the Netherlands and Japan are home to ASML and Tokyo Electron , which make tools used to manufacture semiconductors. The Bill would not directly restrict Nvidia’s chip sales. Supporters argue it could make it more difficult for China to develop its own advanced AI chips to compete with Nvidia in the long term. Remote-access loophole The Remote Access Security Act targets a growing workaround used by Chinese AI companies. Instead of purchasing advanced chips directly, some Chinese firms rent computing power from overseas data centers equipped with Nvidia chips and access the systems remotely. The Bill would give the Commerce Department authority to regulate that activity. The legislation passed the House in January and is awaiting Senate consideration. Among the proposals under consideration, this could have the most direct effect on Nvidia. The company said in July that the measure, if enacted, could have “a material impact on our business.” Reuters reported on Nov 12 that Chinese AI companies are rushing to secure access to Nvidia-powered computing capacity outside China, on concerns that the controversy surrounding Huang could accelerate Washington’s effort to tighten restrictions. REUTERS
